column2: IBM's planned fault-tolerant design built from modules encoded in bivariate bicycle (gross) codes, linked by couplers, with a logical processing unit to perform operations on the stored logical qubits.
column3: In everyday English, a bicycle is a pedal-driven vehicle; the name comes from the bicycle codes it uses.

column2: The coming stage of quantum computing with a small number of error-corrected logical qubits and limited logical operations, between today's noisy devices and full fault tolerance.
An early machine built to demonstrate fault-tolerant quantum computation at small scale, testing the codes, decoders and control needed for larger systems.
A quantum computer that uses error correction so that computations of any length can run reliably, as long as physical error rates are below the threshold.
A connection between separate quantum chips or modules that lets qubits on different modules interact, so a larger computer can be built from smaller pieces.
The time taken to perform one round of logical operations on encoded qubits, including the error correction they need. It sets the speed of a fault-tolerant computer.
A compiler that turns a program into operations on error-corrected logical qubits, such as lattice surgery and magic state use, and schedules them.
The set of operations a fault-tolerant computer can perform directly on its logical qubits, such as logical Clifford gates, measurements and magic state injection.
In IBM's bicycle architecture, the part that performs logical operations, such as measurements of logical Pauli operators, on qubits stored in a code module.
column3: In computing, a processing unit such as a CPU is the part that executes instructions.

column2: A connection that links qubits that are not next to each other on a chip, which some high-rate codes, such as bivariate bicycle codes, need.
Building a large quantum computer from many smaller connected modules, instead of one giant chip, to make manufacturing and scaling easier.
A scheme that protects only some operations or some error types with error correction, trading full protection for fewer qubits.
One round of measuring all the stabilizers of an error-correcting code and processing the results. Its duration limits how fast errors can be caught.
One complete measurement of all the stabilizers of a code, giving a fresh syndrome. Error correction repeats stabilizer rounds continuously.
One round of measuring a code's parity checks to collect a syndrome, the same thing as a stabilizer round.
A subsystem code on a square grid of qubits whose checks are simple two-qubit measurements, making it easy to measure. It protects well against some noise but has no threshold as it grows.
A way of building quantum LDPC codes from two classical codes that share a symmetry, giving codes with better distance than hypergraph products.
A bosonic code that stores a qubit in superpositions of photon-number states with binomial weights, protecting against photon loss.
A family of quantum LDPC codes defined by polynomials in two variables, such as IBM's gross code. They encode many logical qubits with far fewer physical qubits than the surface code.
A code that stores a qubit in the many levels of a harmonic oscillator, such as a microwave cavity, instead of many separate qubits. Cat, binomial and GKP codes are examples.
A bosonic code that stores a qubit in superpositions of two or four coherent states of a resonator. It is strongly protected against bit flips, so only phase flips need further correction.
Encoding each qubit of a code in another code, repeatedly, so that errors are suppressed more at each level. It was used in the first threshold proofs.
A topological code on a lattice with three-colourable faces. It allows all Clifford gates to be applied transversally, but is harder to decode than the surface code.
A scheme that combines cat qubits, which suppress bit flips, with an outer code such as a repetition code that corrects the remaining phase flips.
A code built by encoding the qubits of one code in another code, level by level, so that errors shrink rapidly with each level.
A Calderbank–Shor–Steane code, a stabilizer code built from two classical codes, one handling bit flips and one handling phase flips. The surface and Steane codes are CSS codes.
An encoding of a qubit in which of two modes or resonators holds a single excitation. Losing the excitation leaves both empty, which can be detected as an erasure.
A code whose checks change from round to round, so the protected logical space itself evolves in time. Floquet codes, such as the honeycomb code, are examples.
A quantum LDPC code built with a construction borrowed from the topology of fibre bundles. It was the first to beat the long-standing √n distance barrier for such codes.
The smallest code that corrects any single-qubit error, encoding one logical qubit into five physical qubits with distance three.
A code whose logical qubit is protected by measuring two-qubit checks in a repeating sequence, so the stabilizers change each step. The honeycomb code was the first example.
The smallest code that detects any single-qubit error, encoding two logical qubits in four physical qubits. It detects errors but cannot correct them.
In a subsystem code, an operator that acts on the gauge qubits, which carry no protected information. Measuring gauge operators can give the stabilizers more simply.
A qubit in a subsystem code that is left unprotected and whose state does not matter. Allowing gauge qubits can make syndrome measurement simpler.

The Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill code, which encodes a qubit in an oscillator using grid-like states. It corrects small shifts in position and momentum and is used in photonic and superconducting systems.
IBM's [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code, which stores 12 logical qubits in 144 data qubits with distance 12, about ten times fewer qubits than surface codes need.
column3: In everyday English, gross means disgusting, or 144 (a dozen dozen), the source of the name.

column2: A holographic code by Pastawski, Yoshida, Harlow and Preskill, built from a tiling of perfect tensors. It models how spacetime might emerge in the AdS/CFT correspondence.
An error-correcting code designed for IBM's heavy-hexagon qubit layout, in which each qubit has at most three neighbours. It mixes features of surface and Bacon–Shor codes.
A code built from a network of tensors on a hyperbolic tiling, used as a toy model of how bulk spacetime is encoded on its boundary in quantum gravity.
The first Floquet code, by Hastings and Haah: qubits on a honeycomb lattice with two-qubit checks measured in a repeating three-step pattern.
A surface code on a tiling of a hyperbolic (negatively curved) surface. It can store many more logical qubits per physical qubit than a flat surface code.
A construction that combines two classical codes into a quantum LDPC code. It gives codes with constant rate and distance of about √n.
A construction of quantum LDPC codes using matrices of group elements, which led to codes with good rate and linear distance.
A generalization of bivariate bicycle codes defined with polynomials in more than two variables, giving more design options for high-rate LDPC codes.
The surface code laid out on a flat patch with open boundaries instead of a torus. It stores one logical qubit and is the form built in hardware.
A code that protects a continuous stream of qubits using a repeating encoding pattern, like classical convolutional codes, suited to communication.
A quantum code built from the classical Hamming code, such as the Steane code built from the [7,4] Hamming code.
A low-density parity-check code: a stabilizer code in which each check touches few qubits and each qubit is in few checks. Some encode many logical qubits efficiently.
A quantum code built from classical Reed–Muller codes. Some, such as the 15-qubit code, allow a transversal T gate and are used in magic state distillation.
A quantum LDPC code built on expander graphs that has both constant rate and distance growing linearly with size, a so-called good qLDPC code.
The simplest code: copy a bit into several qubits and take a majority vote. It corrects only one type of error, bit flips or phase flips, but is a common first test.
A surface code laid out at 45 degrees, which reaches the same distance with about half as many qubits. It is the version used in most experiments.
The first quantum error-correcting code, by Peter Shor in 1995. It encodes one qubit in nine and corrects any single-qubit error.
A seven-qubit code by Andrew Steane that corrects any single-qubit error. It is a CSS code with transversal Clifford gates.
A code in which part of the protected space is left unprotected as gauge qubits, which can make measuring the syndrome simpler. The Bacon–Shor code is an example.
A subsystem version of the surface code whose checks are measured with lower-weight operators, simplifying the circuits at some cost in performance.
The leading quantum error-correcting code: qubits on a 2D grid with local four-qubit checks. It has a high threshold of about 1% and needs only nearest-neighbour connections.
Kitaev's code on a lattice wrapped around a torus, the original topological code. It stores two logical qubits, and its excitations behave as anyons.
column3: A torus is a doughnut shape, which is where the name comes from.

column2: A color code on a triangle-shaped patch with boundaries of three colours, storing one logical qubit. The Steane code is the smallest example.
A code with a special structure that allows a transversal T gate, used to distil magic states efficiently.
IBM's [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle code, twice the size of the gross code, storing 12 logical qubits with distance 18.
A surface code variant whose checks are XZZX products. It performs especially well when noise is biased toward one type of error.
Surface code patches linked by extra checks across patches (yokes), which raise the protection of stored qubits using fewer extra qubits than enlarging each patch.
A quasiparticle in two dimensions that is neither a boson nor a fermion; swapping two anyons can change the state by any phase or even a matrix. They underlie topological codes and computing.
An operator measured to detect errors in a code, such as a stabilizer or gauge operator. A flipped result signals that an error occurred nearby.
The smallest number of physical errors that can cause an undetected logical error. A code of distance d can correct up to (d−1)/2 errors.
The number of logical qubits encoded per physical qubit. The surface code has a low rate, while qLDPC codes can have much higher rates.
The subspace of states that a code uses to store information, where all stabilizers have the value +1. Errors push states out of it.
A valid encoded state of a code, one of the states in the code space.
column3: In classical coding theory, a codeword is a valid string of symbols.

column2: Working out, from the syndrome, which errors most likely happened and how to correct them. It must be fast and accurate for error correction to work.
A flipped check result in a syndrome, marking where an error chain starts or ends. It is also used for holes or boundaries cut into a code to store qubits.
column3: In materials science, a defect is a flaw in a crystal, a common source of qubit noise.

column2: A combination of measurement results whose value is fixed in the absence of errors, such as comparing a stabilizer between rounds. Decoders work with detectors that fire.
column3: In everyday English, a detector is any device that senses something, such as a smoke detector.

column2: A description of which detectors each possible error flips, and how likely each error is. It is the input to decoders such as matching.
Spreading the information of logical qubits across many physical qubits, so that errors on a few can be found and fixed.
column3: In computing generally, encoding means converting data into another format.

column2: A string of errors on neighbouring qubits in a topological code. Only its endpoints show up in the syndrome; a chain spanning the code causes a logical error.
Another name for an error chain: a line of errors whose ends light up checks. Strings that cross the whole code act as logical operators.
Keeping a record in software of Pauli corrections that should have been applied, instead of applying them physically, and adjusting later results accordingly.
The rate at which encoded, logical qubits suffer errors after error correction. Below threshold it falls rapidly as the code distance grows.
An operator that changes the encoded logical state while leaving the code space intact, such as logical X or Z. Its minimum weight is the code distance.
A qubit encoded in many physical qubits with error correction, so it is far more reliable than any single physical qubit.
A measurement of whether a group of bits or qubits has an even or odd number of flips. In quantum codes it is a stabilizer measurement.
A matrix whose rows list which bits each parity check involves. It fully describes a classical code and, for CSS codes, the quantum code.
The record of Pauli corrections that have been inferred but not physically applied, tracked in software.
Changing the tracked Pauli frame when a new correction is inferred or a gate transforms it, instead of applying a physical gate.
The error rate of individual physical qubits and operations. It must be below the code's threshold for error correction to help.
A single hardware qubit, such as one transmon or one trapped ion. Many physical qubits make up one logical qubit.
Protecting quantum information by encoding it redundantly across many qubits and repeatedly measuring checks to find and fix errors without disturbing the stored data.
Finding that an error happened without being able to fix it, so the result can be discarded. It needs fewer qubits than full correction.
An operator, usually a product of Paulis, that leaves every valid code state unchanged. Measuring stabilizers reveals errors without revealing the encoded data.
An error-correcting code defined by a group of commuting Pauli stabilizers. Most quantum codes, including the surface code, are stabilizer codes.
A way to describe many-qubit states and codes by the Pauli operators that stabilize them, instead of their exponentially many amplitudes. It makes Clifford circuits easy to track.
One of a minimal set of stabilizers from which all others can be formed by multiplication. Error correction measures the generators.
The group of all Pauli operators that leave the code states unchanged. It is generated by a small set of stabilizer generators.
A state that is the unique +1 eigenstate of a group of Pauli operators, such as a Bell or GHZ state. Such states can be simulated efficiently on classical computers.
The pattern of stabilizer measurement results, which reveals where errors occurred without revealing the encoded information.
Measuring a code's stabilizers, usually with ancilla qubits, to obtain the error syndrome.
The circuit of gates and ancilla measurements used to measure a code's stabilizers each round. Its design affects how errors spread.
Measuring the stabilizers of a code to learn the error syndrome. It must be repeated because measurements themselves can be wrong.
A graph linking qubits (or bits) to the parity checks that involve them. It is used to design and decode LDPC codes.
A point in a topological code where the lattice is twisted so that anyon types swap around it. Twists can store qubits and enable extra logical gates.
A fault-tolerance approach, shown with neutral atoms, in which transversal gates and correlated decoding reduce the number of syndrome rounds needed per logical operation.
A decoder built as a custom chip (application-specific integrated circuit), designed to decode fast and at low power, possibly inside the cryostat.
A decoding algorithm that passes messages between qubits and checks on a Tanner graph to estimate which errors happened. It is fast but needs help, such as OSD, for quantum codes.
Edmonds's algorithm for finding a minimum-weight perfect matching in a graph. It is the classic engine of matching decoders for the surface code.
A decoder that runs belief propagation and, if it fails, uses ordered statistics decoding to find a solution. It is the standard decoder for quantum LDPC codes.
Decoding several logical qubits together, rather than separately, to account for errors that spread between them during transversal gates.
The classical algorithm or hardware that turns syndrome data into a guess of which errors happened, so they can be corrected.
A growing queue of syndrome data that happens when the decoder is slower than the rate at which data arrives. It slows the whole computation exponentially.
The delay between measuring a syndrome and the decoder's answer. Low latency is needed so that corrections are ready before later operations depend on them.
How much syndrome data a decoder can process per second. It must keep pace with the error-correction cycle to avoid a backlog.
A graph whose nodes are detectors and whose edges are possible errors, used by decoders such as matching to find the likeliest errors.
A decoder running on a field-programmable gate array, reconfigurable hardware that can decode quickly and close to the quantum device.
Decoding syndrome data only as far as needed, when a result is about to be used, to keep latency low.
A decoder for qLDPC codes, related to ordered statistics decoding, that splits the problem into small local clusters so they can be decoded in parallel and faster.
A decoder that stores the correction for every possible syndrome in a table. It is very fast but only practical for small codes.
The graph used by a matching decoder, whose nodes are detection events and whose edge weights reflect how likely errors are.
A decoding method that pairs up flipped detectors using the most likely (lowest-weight) set of errors. It is the standard decoder for the surface code.
A decoder that uses a trained neural network to predict corrections from syndromes. It can learn a device's real noise, including correlations.
A decoding method that sorts bits by reliability and solves for the least likely errors among the least reliable bits. It helps belief propagation decode quantum LDPC codes.
Decoding syndromes as fast as they are produced, while the computation runs, which is required for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Decoding a continuous stream of syndrome rounds in overlapping windows, committing to corrections in each window before moving on, so decoding never waits for the whole run.
Decoding that uses how confident each measurement was, not just its 0 or 1 result, to make better decisions.
A decoder that uses tensor network contraction to compute the most likely logical correction almost exactly. It is accurate but slow, used mainly as a benchmark.
A fast decoder that grows clusters around flipped checks until they can be corrected. It runs in almost linear time with accuracy close to matching.
column3: In computer science, union-find is a general data structure for tracking groups.

column2: Operating with physical error rates above a code's threshold, where making the code bigger makes logical errors worse, not better.
Checking that ancilla qubits were prepared correctly before using them in error correction, and discarding bad ones, to avoid spreading errors.
Error correction built into the hardware's physics, for example with engineered dissipation, that fixes errors continuously without measurements and feedback.
When a single fault in a circuit spreads into several errors on data qubits, possibly more than the code can correct. Fault-tolerant circuits are designed to prevent it.
Operating with physical error rates under a code's threshold, so that larger codes give lower logical error rates. It is the key requirement for scalable error correction.
The point at which an error-corrected logical qubit lasts longer, or performs better, than the best physical qubit in the same system.
The physical error rate below which a code's logical error rate falls as the code grows. For the surface code it is about 1% under realistic noise.
A qubit designed so that its main errors are erasures, errors whose location is known, which are much easier to correct than unknown errors.
The spreading of errors through gates, for example a CNOT copying an error from one qubit to another. Fault-tolerant design limits it.
The ability to compute reliably even though individual components are faulty, by designing error correction so that errors do not spread uncontrollably.
column3: In engineering generally, fault tolerance means a system continues working when parts fail.

column2: A logical gate implemented so that one faulty component causes at most a correctable number of errors in each code block.
Measuring a logical qubit or syndrome in a way that a single fault cannot cause an uncorrectable error, for example by repeating it.
Preparing encoded states, such as logical |0⟩, so that a single fault cannot produce an uncorrectable error, often by verifying the result.
Measuring stabilizers in a way that limits error spread from faulty ancillas, using methods such as Shor, Steane, Knill or flag schemes.
An extra qubit that detects when a fault during syndrome measurement has spread into a dangerous multi-qubit error, allowing fault tolerance with few ancillas.
Fault-tolerant syndrome extraction using flag qubits to catch dangerous error spreads, needing far fewer ancillas than older schemes.
A method for turning a stabilizer code into a cluster state for measurement-based fault-tolerant computing, adding a time direction to the code.
column3: In mathematics, a foliation is a way of slicing a space into layers.

column2: An error from a single fault partway through a stabilizer measurement that spreads to several data qubits. Choosing the right gate order limits its damage.
Measuring syndromes by teleporting the data through an encoded Bell pair, which extracts all the error information at once.
Finding qubits that have left the computational states |0⟩ and |1⟩ for higher energy levels, so they can be reset before they corrupt error correction.
A Bell state between two logical qubits, an entangled pair of error-corrected qubits. Preparing it is a benchmark for fault-tolerant hardware.
A gate acting on encoded logical qubits, built from many physical operations so that errors stay correctable.
Measuring the value of an encoded logical qubit, usually by measuring its physical qubits and decoding the result.
The physical error rate at which a specific code of fixed size starts to outperform an unencoded qubit. It differs from the true threshold.
Measuring each stabilizer with a verified cat state of ancillas, so faults cannot spread to several data qubits. It is robust but needs many ancillas.
Error correction that works reliably from a single round of syndrome measurement, without repeating it to catch measurement errors.
Measuring all syndromes at once by coupling the data to a whole encoded ancilla block with transversal gates, then measuring the ancilla.
The theorem that arbitrarily long quantum computations can be performed reliably if physical error rates are below a certain threshold, with only modest overhead.
A logical CNOT between two code blocks made by applying CNOTs between matching physical qubits. It is naturally fault-tolerant because errors cannot spread within a block.
A logical gate built from independent gates on matching physical qubits across code blocks, so a single fault affects at most one qubit per block.
Noise in which one type of error, often phase flips, is far more common than others. Codes such as XZZX or cat qubits can exploit it.
A noise model in which every gate, idle step, preparation and measurement in the syndrome circuit can fail. It is the most realistic standard model.
Simulating error correction with noise on every operation of the actual circuits, to estimate realistic thresholds and logical error rates.
A simplified noise model in which only data qubits suffer errors, once, and syndrome measurement is perfect. It gives the most optimistic thresholds.
An error that affects several qubits at once, for example from crosstalk or cosmic rays. Correlated errors are harder to correct than independent ones.
Noise that replaces the state with a completely random one with some probability, or equivalently applies X, Y or Z errors with equal chance.
Engineering a qubit so that its dominant errors become erasures, detectable errors whose location is known, which codes can correct much more easily.
An error whose location is known, such as a qubit found to have been lost. Codes can correct about twice as many erasures as unknown errors.
When a qubit leaves the computational states |0⟩ and |1⟩ for other levels, such as a transmon's |2⟩. Leaked qubits spread errors and must be detected and reset.
column3: In everyday English, a leakage is fluid or information escaping.

column2: An operation that returns leaked qubits to the computational subspace, applied regularly during error correction so leakage does not build up.
A wrong measurement result, reading 0 as 1 or the reverse. In error correction it is why syndromes must be measured repeatedly.
A noise model in which errors are random Pauli operators (X, Y, Z) applied with some probabilities. It is easy to simulate and many real noises can be twirled into it.
A noise model in which data qubits have errors and syndrome measurements can also be wrong, but the gates inside the syndrome circuits are ideal.
An experiment showing that increasing the code distance lowers the logical error rate, proving hardware operates below threshold. Google showed this with its Willow chip in 2024.
The number of physical qubits needed per logical qubit, or for a whole algorithm. Lowering the footprint is a major goal of new codes.
column3: In everyday English, a footprint is the mark left by a foot, or the space something takes up.

column2: The factor by which the logical error rate drops each time the code distance increases by two. A value above 1 means the code is working below threshold.
column3: In physics and mathematics, lambda (λ) is used for many other quantities, such as wavelength.

column2: How many logical operations per second a fault-tolerant computer can perform, set by the error-correction cycle time and decoding speed.
The drop in logical error rate achieved by error correction, ideally exponential in the code distance when running below threshold.
How long a logical qubit keeps its information under error correction before a logical error occurs.
The lifetime of an encoded logical qubit, the logical counterpart of a physical qubit's T1 relaxation time.
An experiment that stores a logical qubit under repeated error correction and measures how quickly logical errors occur. It is the standard first test of a code.
An experiment running a repetition code to test error correction against one type of error, a simpler step before full codes.
Calculating how many physical qubits, how much time and how many operations a fault-tolerant algorithm will need on given hardware.
The number of physical qubits multiplied by the time they are used. It measures the total cost of a fault-tolerant operation or algorithm.
The extra qubits and time that error correction adds compared with an ideal computation, measured as space-time volume.
The number of layers of T gates in a circuit when T gates that can run at the same time are grouped. It limits run time on fault-tolerant hardware.
The result that transversal or constant-depth logical gates on 2D topological codes are limited to the Clifford hierarchy's third level, restricting which gates are cheap.
The theorem that no quantum error-correcting code can implement a universal set of logical gates transversally. Extra methods, such as magic states, are always needed.
The theorem that circuits of Clifford gates, Pauli measurements and stabilizer states can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer.
The necessary and sufficient conditions for a quantum code to correct a set of errors: errors must not distinguish codewords or disturb them differently.
An upper limit on how many logical qubits a code can store while correcting a given number of errors, for non-degenerate codes.
A limit on quantum codes: the number of physical qubits minus logical qubits must be at least 2(d − 1), where d is the distance.
Moving anyons around each other so their paths form braids. The result depends only on the braid's topology, which makes it a robust way to perform gates.
Moving quasiparticles or code defects around each other to perform logical operations. In topological codes, braiding defects implements gates.
column3: In everyday English, braiding is weaving strands of hair or rope together.

column2: A fault-tolerant scheme that performs only Clifford gates on encoded qubits. It is easy to protect but not universal without magic states.
Changing the shape or checks of a code step by step to move, split or merge logical qubits, performing logical operations without leaving the code.
Converting encoded qubits from one code to another, for example to use each code's easy transversal gates, getting a universal gate set.
A dedicated area of a fault-tolerant computer that continuously produces high-quality magic states through distillation for use in T gates.
A magic state distillation protocol that takes 15 noisy T states and outputs one much cleaner one, based on the 15-qubit Reed–Muller code.
A 2019 paper by Daniel Litinski describing fault-tolerant computing with the surface code as a board game of patches and lattice surgery, a widely used design framework.
A way to perform logical operations between surface code patches by temporarily merging and splitting their boundaries, needing only nearest-neighbour operations.
A region of qubits encoding one or more logical qubits in a code such as the surface code, which can be moved and merged with lattice surgery.
A special non-stabilizer state, such as the T state, that lets a Clifford-only machine perform a non-Clifford gate by consuming it.
A 2024 method by Gidney, Shutty and Jones that grows a high-quality magic state inside a surface code patch, far more cheaply than traditional distillation.
Turning many noisy magic states into fewer, cleaner ones using error-detecting codes, so fault-tolerant T gates can be performed.
Preparing a magic state on physical qubits and encoding it into a logical qubit, the first, noisy step before distillation.
The two basic steps of lattice surgery: merging code patches measures a joint logical operator, and splitting them apart again completes the operation.
A section of a surface code lattice that stores a logical qubit. Computations are carried out by moving, merging and splitting patches.
column3: In everyday English, a patch is a small piece of material used to mend something.

column2: The code distance against errors spreading across the qubits of a code at one moment, set by the patch size.
A region of a fault-tolerant computer that produces T-type magic states, usually by distillation or cultivation.
Preparing a noisy T state and encoding it into a code, to be improved and then consumed to perform a T gate.
The code distance against errors spreading in time, such as repeated measurement errors, set by how many rounds of syndrome measurement are repeated.
A set of fault-tolerant logical operations, such as transversal Clifford gates plus magic-state T gates, that together can perform any quantum computation.
